To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The very largest observed events on Twitter are almost always highly viral; (2) However, many smaller events, with thousands of adopters, exhibit surprising structural diversity, growing through both viral and non-viral mechanisms; (3) These empirical results are largely explained by a simple contagion process on a scale-free social network.

(1) the largest observed viral events are nearly all highly structurally viral, and (2) medium-sized events exhibit surprising structural diversity and can spread through either broadcast or viral mechanisms.
(1) the most viral products and ideas are those that grow through multiple generations of diffusion and (2) the most viral of these events are those that are also the most popular.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the structural properties of the diffusion process that drives the spread of popular content, and the factors that contribute to the virality of an idea or product.
understanding the structure of the social network that supports viral growth, and how this structure relates to the popularity of the viral event.
the fundamental question: What makes a viral event viral?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most viral of viral products and ideas are indeed viral, but many other popular events are not.
viral diffusion does not explain all of the growth of all products and ideas, but that it is a significant factor in the growth of many of them.
the structural virality of a given event is not only an important property, but also a very useful one for understanding how and why that event grew.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the structural virality of online diffusion is a key determinant of a product or idea’s popularity.
viral products and ideas grow primarily through a person-to- person diffusion process, but that this is not the only way that they grow.

the viral growth of online content is a complex process with both viral and broadcast components, and that the structural properties of the resulting viral events are largely consistent with simple contagion spreading on a scale free network.
